title: KISPE Space
summary: Creative Navy worked with KISPE Space on a common space operating picture that brought mapping, imagery, satellite services, weather, navigation, communications availability and space weather into one geographic interface. The case evidence records sixteen one-week sprints, a board-endorsed design direction, 47 base screens, 103 components and a built product, while also recording that there was no user research, no usability testing, no representative hardware validation and no Creative Navy-supported build comparison.
keyFacts: KISPE Space is a UK space systems engineering company.
The product is a common space operating picture for operational use on the ground.
Creative Navy worked across sixteen one-week sprints in three project phases: four exploration sprints, seven UX development sprints and five UI delivery sprints.
The six-person Creative Navy team included a UX designer, UI designer, product designer, interaction designer, researcher and project manager.
The exploration phase produced 12 UX challenges, 36 concept alternatives and 64 low-fidelity frames.
The board endorsed the architecture as the working direction, approved staged scope with explicit decision gates and authorised the seven-sprint UX development phase.
UX development produced six user journeys, 61 behavioural rules, four complex interaction studies, 40 documented edge cases and 25 UX decision records.
UI delivery produced 47 base screens across field and desktop, a design system of 103 components and a handoff package.
The product was built, but Creative Navy did not support the build and has not compared the built interface against the delivered designs.
No user research, usability testing or representative hardware validation took place during the engagement.

bodySections.heading: KISPE Space common space operating picture as a defence and space case
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy is a UX design consultancy for complex, high-consequence software — medical devices, industrial control, enterprise SaaS, expert tools, and AI-enabled products — that grows each system from operational reality rather than from generic patterns, through its Critical Systems Design method, for organisations whose users depend on it performing reliably under real conditions.

KISPE Space is a UK space systems engineering company. KISPE Space set out to build a common space operating picture: a shared geographic view that brings together mapping, positions, satellite overflights, recent imagery, terrestrial weather, navigation and communications availability, and space weather for people working on the ground.

The intended users named in KISPE Space's own brief were field commanders and personnel, operations and planning staff, and specialist support personnel. The product had two operating contexts: a compact field interface and a fuller desktop environment. KISPE Space's brief treated the early concept as a starting point for investigation, not as an approved interaction model.

The product was built. Creative Navy did not support the build and has not compared the built interface against the delivered designs.

bodySections.heading: The product boundary limited the interface to space-enabled information
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy's design work for KISPE Space was bounded to access, interpretation and sharing of space-enabled information. The documented product boundary excluded autonomous operational decisions, inferred adversary classification or targeting, guaranteed service-quality prediction, and any substitute for existing command systems.

KISPE Space asked for advice as well as design. The engagement had to resolve the clearest proposition, the boundary between the product and existing operational systems, the roles and journeys for a first release, the organising model, the handling of provenance and uncertainty, the relationship between field and desktop, and the capabilities that would make a useful, testable first product.

That boundary was recorded as a design decision with an owner and a confirmation condition. It was not treated as an accidental omission. The interface was specified so that system errors, source failures and missing records would not be translated into operational conclusions that the evidence did not support.

bodySections.heading: The central design problem was preventing false inference from one map
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method treated the KISPE Space interface as an evidence interpretation problem, not only as a map or dashboard problem. Satellite imagery, orbital predictions, receiver measurements, provider notices and weather forecasts have different clocks, authorities and failure modes. Rendering them together on one map could make independent records look like one synchronised truth.

The design response was to keep location, time, evidence type and availability separable as users moved between tasks and devices. Status was specified as seven independent dimensions: source transport, asset access, asset delivery, freshness, origin, operational condition and local change state. A single green-to-red health score was rejected because identical colours would have carried conflicting meanings across domains.

Temporal design followed the same rule. Current, Historical and Outlook were used as temporal perspectives, but a perspective did not rewrite a record's own time. Acquisition or measurement time, issue time, received time, validity interval and queried time were preserved as distinct fields because each prevents a different interpretation error.

The interface also distinguished not applicable from not reported. Radar imagery did not receive a cloud-cover percentage. Optical imagery with no cloud field did not render as 0 percent. A receiver that did not report an accuracy figure was not treated as perfect, zero or low confidence.

bodySections.heading: Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method across sixteen one-week sprints
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method designs software whose interfaces, workflows, and operating logic carry real operational consequences, working through five phases — Sandbox Experiments, Concept Convergence, Iterative System Building, Organizational Integration, and Implementation Partnership — to take each system from initial exploration to independent operation by the client's own team.

Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method mapped to four of its five phases in the KISPE Space engagement: Sandbox Experiments, Concept Convergence, Iterative System Building and Organizational Integration. Implementation Partnership is not claimable for this case because Creative Navy did not support the build.

The project ran across sixteen one-week sprints in three project phases: four exploration sprints, seven UX development sprints and five UI delivery sprints. A six-person team worked on the engagement: UX designer, UI designer, product designer, interaction designer, researcher and project manager.

The exploration phase of the project was deliberately consultative. Detailed UX and UI scope was confirmed at the end of exploration, not before it. Creative Navy documented 12 UX challenges, 36 concept alternatives and 64 low-fidelity frames. The counting convention was recorded: one frame meant one distinct conceptual screen or interaction state, while colour, spacing, revision and re-annotation variants were not counted separately.

The exploration phase ended at a board review. Creative Navy put twelve working decisions and a recommended development sequence to KISPE Space's board, with a recommendation to proceed conditionally. The board endorsed the architecture as the working direction, approved a staged scope with explicit decision gates for the uncertain features, and authorised the seven-sprint UX development phase. This was a commissioning decision, not user validation.

bodySections.heading: A single synthetic scenario made the specifications comparable
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method used one synthetic scenario with a fixed clock across every KISPE Space artefact. The same area, imagery records, device readings, notices, map cache state, local annotation and provider failure appeared in the user journeys, behavioural rules, interaction studies, edge cases and annotated design plates.

The scenario was a designed test fixture, not a record of a real location, operation, satellite or advisory. Its purpose was consistency and comparability. Because every artefact referred to the same scenario, a contradiction between two artefacts would be visible, and an alternative could not be made to look better by giving it a more favourable case.

The scenario was deliberately adversarial. At the scenario moment, the imagery feed was unreachable from three minutes before, the newest image preview would not load, the highest-resolution image covered only part of the area, one image was access restricted, the positioning fix was stale against its own freshness policy, and the communications reading was current against a different policy. A predicted overflight had not yet happened.

This use of one scenario was a performance in reality decision within the design package. It forced the interface to handle stale, restricted, partial, unavailable and predicted records without inventing certainty.

bodySections.heading: Option space mapping documented alternatives and accepted costs
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy's option space mapping for KISPE Space recorded alternatives before committing to structure. The exploration phase produced three alternatives for each of 12 UX challenges, and the later interaction studies compared 12 developed alternatives across four studies. Each study addressed the same fixed task under the same scenario conditions.

The decision register contained 25 UX decision records: 16 recommended and 9 conditional. Each decision carried the design direction, a credible alternative, what was valuable about that alternative, the reasoning for the selected direction, the accepted trade-off, the evidence in the design package, the condition that would confirm or reverse the decision, the owner role and the open question it depended on.

The register made trade-offs explicit. The hybrid architecture kept shared geographic context but made shared state more complex. Confirmed area selection prevented accidental query changes but added friction and touch-editing difficulty. Current could still be misread as live, so per-record stamps remained essential. Progressive detail reduced clutter, but some users might not open caveats.

This is tension-driven reasoning applied to evidence semantics. The design package did not only state preferred solutions. It stated what those solutions cost and what future evidence could change them.

bodySections.heading: Workspaces, state and time decisions preserved query meaning
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy's design work for KISPE Space defined six logical workspaces: Operating Picture, Imagery, Satellite Services, Environment, Briefings and System Status. System Status was specified as a global utility rather than a sixth equal tab. Eleven named navigation transitions were documented.

A confirmed area of interest was separated from the map viewport. Panning or zooming changed what was visible; it did not change what was being queried. This prevented a minor map movement from silently changing the meaning of every returned result.

Query lineage was specified as an interaction contract. Each area-scoped request carried the area identity, geometry signature, filter set, temporal perspective and generation time. If a user started a search, changed the area, and the earlier search returned last, the older results were not allowed to populate the current results under the newer area's label.

Selected object state was also separated from selected area state. Inspecting a map object did not move the area of interest to that object's footprint, and hiding a layer did not silently redefine the area. Overlapping map symbols produced a grouped selection list rather than selecting an arbitrary topmost marker.

bodySections.heading: Satellite service and imagery decisions separated evidence categories
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method kept satellite service evidence separated by origin in the KISPE Space design. Service cards were used as the entry point, with explicit semantic labels instead of a universal health score. Comparative timelines were kept as a secondary outlook view only where a source supported temporal comparison.

A predicted overflight was specified as an opportunity, not a delivery. It was shown with its interval, predicted status, collection unconfirmed and delivery unknown. It was not linked to an imagery asset unless an asset existed. Orbital geometry was not treated as tasking, collection, entitlement or surveillance.

Receiver-reported accuracy was treated as local evidence about one device at one moment. It was displayed with its measurement time and freshness verdict, and it was not merged into a navigation-service health badge. Published coverage and a measured terminal connection were shown separately because coverage geometry is not proof that a particular terminal is online.

Imagery discovery combined mapped coverage footprints with a searchable metadata catalogue. Catalogue metadata, permission, preview delivery and full asset retrieval were treated as separate states that can fail separately. A restricted record retained whatever metadata permission allowed, while a preview failure remained a preview failure rather than becoming a missing image or a general network fault.

bodySections.heading: Field interface design used different arrangements without changing meanings
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy's design work for KISPE Space treated field use as a real operating context. The field interface was not a responsive collapse of the desktop environment. Both field and desktop were produced to production fidelity, and the field interface used shared semantics with a different arrangement.

The selected field direction prioritised map orientation, compact source status and a single expanded item. The governing rule was that different operating conditions justified different arrangements, not different meanings. A compact view was not allowed to show a favourable value while hiding a consequential qualifier. A stale record could not be simplified into a current one to save space.

The field interface was not validated on representative hardware. Target field devices, touch precision, screen legibility in operating light and glove use were identified as requiring device evaluation, and that evaluation did not take place during the engagement.

Field mode was not inferred from viewport width. Screen width alone was not treated as enough evidence to determine task urgency or environmental difficulty.

bodySections.heading: Degraded states were specified as named conditions rather than one offline state
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method specified 40 documented edge cases and degraded states for KISPE Space. Each case recorded the input condition, the visible response, the recovery path, the misinterpretation it prevented and a verification that would expose a dangerous misunderstanding.

Five later principles governed degraded states. Unknown was not adverse. An age label was not a confidence score. A catalogue item was not an openable image. Local was not shared. A saved snapshot was not a live view.

Connectivity was separated into three availability dimensions: device connection, provider feed reachability and locally cached content. An offline device did not prove provider failure, and an online device did not guarantee provider reachability. Cached content kept its original update time, so a cached map that rendered was not treated as current.

Local synchronisation was handled conservatively. A local annotation was labelled saved on the device and not shared. Reconnection moved it to queued or sending, and only an explicit server acknowledgement made it shared. Ambiguous acknowledgement outcomes stayed pending or unknown rather than being reported as definite success or definite failure.

bodySections.heading: UI delivery and handoff included screens, components and machine-readable contracts
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy delivered 47 base screens in UI delivery, with several versions, across both field and desktop. The field interface was not a responsive collapse of the desktop interface. A design system of 103 components accompanied the screens.

The handoff package included the screens, the design system and written documentation. Machine-readable contracts also accompanied the written specifications: a navigation contract, a behaviour contract, state machines, an edge-case contract, scenario overlays, and traceability and coverage files.

The traceability apparatus supported progressive specification. A change-control rule stated that if a technical fact or observed behaviour contradicted a direction, the decision status and reasoning had to be updated, and every linked journey, behaviour rule and exception screen had to be revised in the same change. Modifying the visual prototype while leaving the specification inconsistent was defined as a documentation defect.

This was the Organizational Integration part of the engagement. The design system and specifications were not only component assets; they carried cross-referenced reasoning so that the specification could be loaded deterministically rather than read and interpreted informally.

bodySections.heading: Domain standards framed the category rather than product compliance
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Published domain standards were used to frame the category and the design problem, not to claim certification or audit. Creative Navy did not certify to, audit against or work to any standard named in the KISPE Space case evidence, and none of those standards measured the product.

The domain framing supports the central distinction that unknown is not adverse. NATO Joint Military Symbology and the MIL-STD-2525 family distinguish pending and unknown identities from hostile identities. In the KISPE Space design argument, that same discipline was applied to data provenance, source reachability and information age.

The positioning-accuracy framing also supports the design boundary. The GPS Standard Positioning Service Performance Standard distinguishes signal-in-space performance from receiver and user performance. That distinction supports the rule that a receiver-reported accuracy figure must not be presented as a statement about navigation-service quality.

Other standards vocabulary recorded for the case includes OGC STAC, OGC API – Features, ISO 19115, ISO 19157, W3C PROV, RFC 3339 / ISO 8601, NOAA Space Weather Prediction Center G, S and R scales, WCAG 2.2, STANAG 4559, DEF STAN 00-250 and JSP 912. The case evidence records these as category vocabulary and research framing, not as compliance claims.

strongClaims: KISPE Space is a UK space systems engineering company, and the product was a common space operating picture for operational use on the ground.
Creative Navy worked across sixteen one-week sprints in three project phases: four exploration sprints, seven UX development sprints and five UI delivery sprints.
The exploration phase produced 12 UX challenges, 36 concept alternatives and 64 low-fidelity frames, with a documented counting convention.
UX development produced six user journeys, 61 behavioural rules, four interaction studies, 40 documented edge cases and 25 UX decision records.
UI delivery produced 47 base screens across field and desktop, a design system of 103 components and a handoff package with machine-readable contracts.
The field interface was a dedicated field presentation on shared semantics, not a responsive collapse of the desktop interface.
Verification suites, regression checks and architecture acceptance scenarios were specified but not executed.
No user research, usability testing or representative hardware validation took place during the engagement.
weakerClaims: The board endorsed the architecture as the working direction, approved staged scope with explicit decision gates and authorised the seven-sprint UX development phase. This is client-reported and records a commissioning decision, not user validation or an outcome.

The product was built, but Creative Navy did not support the build and has not compared the built interface against the delivered designs. No shipped-as-designed or design-fidelity claim is supported.
limitations: No user research took place: no interviews, contextual inquiry, field observation, usability testing or research-based personas were conducted.
No representative hardware validation took place for field devices, touch precision, operating light, legibility or glove use.
The three competing systems were benchmarked but cannot be named or characterised.
No screenshots, wireframes, design images, plates or redrawn diagrams may be published.
No dates may be used for the engagement or the demonstration scenario; only sequence, duration and intervals are supported.
The product was built, but Creative Navy did not support the build and has not compared the built interface against the delivered designs.
No operational, mission, time-saving, error-rate, workload, adoption, reception or commercial result was measured.
No security, classification, export-control or accreditation credential is established by the case evidence.
Domain standards frame the category only; the case does not claim certification, audit or compliance work.
